source_refs.note: Topic 20.2 with the Did You Know box and Quick Check 20.2, answered (PDF 62-64); the structures are redrawn. The Did You Know figure labels the 1,4-isomer 'ortho (1,3)'; it is para (1,4). The answers depend on reading the printed drawings and need review.

blocks.text: Aromatic hydrocarbons with only one benzene ring are monocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. Benzene derivatives are named in two styles: with the word benzene as the base name, or with a special name.

items: Most are named with the base name benzene and the substituent as a prefix, e.g. chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene and methylbenzene.
Many have common names that IUPAC accepts as base names, e.g. phenol, toluene and aniline. A single substituent is always on C-1, so no number is needed.
Some have special names accepted by IUPAC, e.g. benzenecarboxylic acid and benzenesulphonic acid.

blocks.alt: Nine benzene rings, each with one substituent, named as in the book: toluene (methylbenzene), phenol (benzenol), anisole (methoxybenzene), aniline (benzenamine), benzaldehyde (benzenecarbaldehyde), benzoic acid (benzenecarboxylic acid), benzene sulphonic acid, nitrobenzene and chlorobenzene.
blocks.caption: Common names of monosubstituted benzenes (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 62-63).

items: The carbon carrying the higher-priority substituent is C-1, and the others are numbered from it. The order of priority is: -COOH > -CN > -CHO > -COCH3 > -OH > -NH2 > -OR > -R.
If both substituents have the same priority, the one first in the alphabet is on C-1, e.g. 1-bromo-2-chlorobenzene.

blocks.alt: Three disubstituted benzenes with numbered ring carbons: 3-hydroxybenzoic acid (COOH on C-1, OH on C-3; acid is higher priority than alcohol), 4-isopropylphenol, also 4-(1-methylethyl)-phenol (OH on C-1, isopropyl on C-4; the phenol alcohol is C-1), and 1-bromo-2-chlorobenzene (Br on C-1, Cl on C-2; bromo is before chloro in the alphabet).
blocks.caption: Names of disubstituted benzenes (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 63).

blocks.title: Did you know? Ortho, meta and para
blocks.text: When there are two substituents, ortho- (o-), meta- (m-) and para- (p-) can be used instead of numbers: ortho means positions 1,2, meta 1,3 and para 1,4. For example, 1,4-dibromobenzene is para-dibromobenzene.

blocks.alt: Three dibromobenzenes with ring carbons numbered 1 to 6: Br on C-1 and C-2 labelled ortho (1,2), Br on C-1 and C-3 labelled meta (1,3), and Br on C-1 and C-4 labelled para (1,4).
blocks.caption: Ortho, meta and para positions of benzene (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 63).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed drawing labels 1,4-dibromobenzene 'ortho (1,3)'; bromine atoms at positions 1 and 4 are para (1,4), as drawn above.
Aromatic hydrocarbons with two or more benzene rings in the molecule are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, e.g. naphthalene (C10H8), anthracene (C14H10) and phenanthrene (C14H10).

blocks.alt: Kekule structures of naphthalene, two fused rings (C10H8); anthracene, three rings in a straight line (C14H10); and phenanthrene, three rings joined at an angle (C14H10).
blocks.caption: Three polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (original structures after the book's examples).
blocks.long_description: In polycyclic arenes neighbouring rings share a C-C edge. Anthracene and phenanthrene have the same formula, C14H10, but their rings are joined differently: in a line and at an angle.

blocks.text: Give names to the following arenes:

blocks.alt: Six arenes numbered i to vi: (i) benzene with NO2 groups on C-1 and C-3; (ii) with Cl on two neighbouring carbons; (iii) with OH and Br opposite each other; (iv) with CH3, a Cl next to it and a Cl opposite it; (v) with CH3 and three NO2 groups at the two neighbouring carbons and the opposite carbon; (vi) benzene carrying C(=O)-O-CH3.
